docs.title: SMINT: Spatial Multi-Omics Integration
docs.text: SMINT brings spatial omics modalities into one coordinate system. It segments cells and nuclei across whole-slide images, then registers spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics and post-stain imaging onto each other — interactively in napari, from the command line, or as SLURM jobs.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
SMINT is installed from GitHub (it is not on PyPI). Python 3.10+:

pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

STalign, used for sequential-section registration, and napari, for the interactive plugin, are installed separately — see Installation.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
Two registration regimes, chosen by how the modalities were acquired:

Situation Method Sequential sections — modalities from different physical sections STalign LDDMM, guided by manual landmarks Same section, post-staining — a second modality on the exact same section Correspondence fitting: affine, RANSAC or thin-plate spline

Spatial metabolomics (MALDI, pink) registered onto Xenium spatial transcriptomics (blue) from a neighbouring section: 11 paired landmarks guide STalign LDDMM. Venture 5, Z2 / Ven5B; rendered with examples/registration_figures.py.

  • napari plugin — load datasets, pre-register by eye (scale, rotate, flip), place paired landmarks, and launch registration without leaving the viewer. Open Plugins → SMINT Registration. See napari Plugin.

  • smint-alignment CLI — the same machinery from the shell:

    # Sequential sections: STalign LDDMM from saved landmarks
smint-alignment st-sm --st st.csv --sm sm.csv \
    --st-points st_points.npy --sm-points sm_points.npy --output-dir run1

# Same section: fit nuclei centroids onto Xenium cells
smint-alignment centroid --source nuclei.csv --target xenium.csv --output-dir run2

# Coarse scale / rotate / flip, searching orientations by overlap
smint-alignment pretransform --source sm.csv --target xenium.csv --search --output sm_pre.csv

  • Honest metrics — Target Registration Error is reported on held-out pairs, so a flexible transform cannot flatter itself by memorising correspondences.

  • HPC native — add --submit to run on SLURM (CPU or GPU) instead of locally; napari submits the same jobs and polls them in the background.

See Alignment for the full workflow.

docs.title: Spatial Alignment
docs.text:
SMINT aligns spatial omics modalities in two quite different situations, and picking the right one matters more than any parameter you will tune afterwards.

Situation What is true Use Sequential sections — the modalities come from different physical sections The tissue genuinely differs between them; no cell corresponds one-to-one STalign LDDMM (register_sm_to_st) Same section, post-staining — a second modality is acquired on the exact same section Centroids really do correspond one-to-one Correspondence fitting (register_centroids)

Using the same-section tools on sequential sections will happily produce a number, but it will be fitting noise: nearest-neighbour "correspondences" between different sections pair cells that are merely nearby, not the same.

docs.title: Coarse pre-registration
docs.text:
Spatial metabolomics arrives on its own pixel grid, frequently rotated or mirrored relative to the Xenium section and at a completely different scale. LDDMM will not recover from a gross orientation mismatch, so bring the datasets roughly together first.

from smint.alignment import build_pretransform, apply_pretransform, overlap_score

matrix = build_pretransform(
    sm_xy, xen_xy,
    scale_mode="extent",   # match bounding-box spans
    rotation=30,           # degrees counter-clockwise
    flip_x=True,
)
moved = apply_pretransform(sm_xy, matrix)
print(overlap_score(moved, xen_xy))     # 0-1, higher is better

Operations are applied in a fixed order — flip → rotate → scale → translate — about the source centroid. The order is fixed because rotations and flips do not commute.

Scale is fitted after orientation is corrected

Bounding-box extents change under rotation, so fitting scale on the raw source bakes in an error. On a 30° rotated test shape, fitting first gave 8.10 against a true 10.0. build_pretransform handles this for you by applying flip and rotation before fitting.

scale_mode options:

  • "extent" (default) — match the bounding-box span per axis. Robust to the two datasets having different origins.
  • "max" — match maximum coordinates directly. Literal, but wrong whenever either dataset does not start near zero.
  • "none" — no scaling.

Scaling is isotropic by default (preserve_aspect=True). Anisotropic scaling can force bounding boxes to agree while making the shapes match worse, which then misleads the landmark step.

Use describe_pretransform(matrix) to decompose a transform into scale, rotation, shear and whether it reflects — a negative determinant means a reflection crept in, which is easy to introduce by combining a flip with a rotation.

docs.title: ST-SM registration
docs.text: For sequential sections, using STalign's LDDMM. The workflow is deliberately split into two phases around a manual landmark step, because that step is where the biological judgement lives.

docs.title: Phase 1 — prepare landmark inputs
docs.text:
from smint.alignment import prepare_landmark_inputs

out = prepare_landmark_inputs(
    st_file="Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv",
    sm_file="Ven5B_information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv",
    output_prefix="/path/to/ven5_z2",
    dx=30.0,
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=10.0, rotate_left_90=True),
)

This writes <prefix>_st.npz and <prefix>_sm.npz.

docs.title: Phase 2 — annotate, then register
docs.text:
Annotate both .npz files, picking the same anatomical features in the same order in each — correspondence is positional, so an ordering mismatch silently produces a wrong registration. Either use the napari plugin or STalign's standalone annotator (STalign/point_annotator.py in the STalign repository — it is not part of SMINT):

python point_annotator.py ven5_z2_st.npz ven5_z2_sm.npz

That writes <prefix>_st_points.npy and <prefix>_sm_points.npy. Then:

from smint.alignment import register_sm_to_st

df = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file=..., sm_file=...,
    st_points_file=out["st_points"],
    sm_points_file=out["sm_points"],
    output_path="sm_transformed.csv",
    niter=1000, epV=200.0,
    orientation="stalign",   # x/y in the ST frame; see below
)

docs.title: Choosing which columns to register
docs.text:
ST tables routinely carry several coordinate pairs from successive processing stages — x_centroid alongside x_new and x_new_add, say. Which one you register against is a real choice, and the wrong one misregisters silently rather than raising.

Inspect first:

smint-alignment columns Ven5_z2_pre_aligned_1.csv

Then be explicit:

register_sm_to_st(
    ..., st_x_col="x_new_add", st_y_col="y_new_add",
    sm_kwargs=dict(x_col="x", y_col="y"),
)

smint-alignment st-sm ... --st-x-col x_new_add --st-y-col y_new_add

Omitting them auto-detects in the priority order x_final, x_centroid, centroid_x, x_transformed, x — and logs the choice, so it appears in the job log. In the napari plugin the columns are dropdowns populated from the file you pick, with the detected pair preselected.

docs.title: Coordinate orientation
docs.text:
STalign works in row-column order throughout. LDDMM takes grids as [Y, X], and transform_points_source_to_target both accepts and returns points as (row, col) — it applies the transform in place and does not transpose.

Registering through STalign therefore returns coordinates whose axes are transposed relative to the source dataset. transform_points exposes this:

  • orientation="stalign" — true x/y in the ST target frame. Use this whenever the result is overlaid on, compared with or joined to the ST data.
  • orientation="dataset" (default) — the transposed layout earlier pipeline runs wrote. It reproduces historical outputs, so existing downstream code keeps working, but these coordinates do not line up with the ST cells.

The two differ by a transpose. Plotting dataset output over ST gives a mirrored, misaligned overlay that looks like a failed registration, so pass the orientation explicitly; it is recorded on the output frame.

docs.title: Centroid registration
docs.text:
For post-staining on the same section, where centroids correspond one-to-one.

from smint.alignment import register_centroids

result = register_centroids(nucleus_xy, xenium_xy)   # method="multiround"
print(result["tre_validation"])                       # the number that matters
print(result["validation"]["after"])                  # median NN, matched fractions

Method What it does multiround (default) Coarse-to-fine displacement voting: an affine, then optional smooth TPS rounds affine Least-squares affine on all nearest-neighbour pairs ransac RANSAC-robust affine; rejects bad correspondences tps Thin-plate spline after an affine pre-alignment ransac+tps RANSAC affine, then TPS on the inliers

docs.title: Why multiple rounds
docs.text:
The single-round methods match every nucleus to its nearest cell once, before fitting. When the starting offset is comparable to the cell spacing, most of those matches are wrong, and no transform fitted to them can recover: on Venture 5 z5 (cells ~17 µm apart, nuclei ~12 µm off) they barely move the alignment.

multiround never commits to nearest neighbours. Within each block of tissue, every nucleus votes for the displacements to several nearby cells; wrong candidates scatter, while the true offset — shared by the whole block — piles up as a peak (vote_block_displacements). Then:

  1. Round 1 fits an affine through the block peaks (500 µm blocks).
  2. Round 2 votes again in 250 µm blocks on the result and adds a smooth TPS through those peaks, following local warps.
  3. A round is kept only if it improves the fitting nuclei's alignment; otherwise registration stops there.

(a) In one block the nearest-cell offsets (white) cluster around zero, but the votes peak at the true offset of (23, 5) µm — more than a cell spacing. (b) The block peaks across the section form a smooth field (a small rotation and scale), which round 1 fits as an affine; red crosses are blocks that disagree and are ignored. © The same window after the old one-shot fit and after multiround. (d) Held-out nuclei: distance to the nearest cell. (e) The finer TPS round didn't improve this section, so it was rejected. examples/multiround_figure.py renders this figure.

Each round's outcome is in result["rounds"]. Tune with schedule= — (max_distance, block_size, bin_size) per round, in microns — and min_improvement=.

Venture 5 z5, held-out nuclei median NN matched ≤ 5 µm matched ≤ 10 µm no transform 12.4 µm 10% 34% ransac+tps (one round) 11.5 µm 13% 40% multiround 5.4 µm 45% 76%

Matched = mutual nearest neighbours. 88,906 nuclei, 74,247 cells; 3 s.

docs.title: Snapping matched nuclei onto their cells
docs.text:
A smooth transform leaves every nucleus a few microns from its cell — partly because a stained nucleus genuinely sits off-centre in its Xenium cell. To make matched nuclei overlap their cells exactly, register_centroid_files (and so smint-alignment centroid) follows registration with refine_by_assignment, a port of the lab's alignment_refinement.r:

  1. Pair registered nuclei one-to-one with Xenium cells (mutual nearest neighbours within snap_radius, 10 µm).
  2. Check each pair against its neighbourhood: its offset must be within consistency_tol (default 0.4 × the cell spacing) of the median offset of the pairs around it. A nucleus paired with the wrong cell disagrees with its neighbours.
  3. Snap pairs that pass: the nucleus moves exactly onto its cell.
  4. Fill in every other nucleus with the median offset of its nearest snapped neighbours; nuclei with none within 100 µm stay put.
  5. Repeat pairing for what is left, up to four passes.
  6. Assign the nuclei still left to the free cells around them by a one-to-one, minimum-total-distance assignment (within 0.75 × the cell spacing), and move them onto those cells. These skipped the neighbourhood check, so they are marked assigned rather than snapped.

On Venture 5 z5, 65,349 nuclei — 88% of Xenium cells — end up exactly on a distinct cell: 57,083 snapped and 8,266 assigned. 9,147 follow their neighbours, and 14,410 lie outside the Xenium area (median 250 µm from any cell). On synthetic sections with known correspondence, the passes snap 98% of the nuclei that have a cell, and 98% of snaps are on the right one.

Assigned pairs are not verified

Each placed nucleus has a neighbour_deviation: how far its offset is from the median offset of the snapped nuclei around it. Right pairs sit at the nucleus-in-cell scatter; a nucleus put on a neighbour's cell deviates by about a cell spacing. On z5 the snapped pairs' median is 4.1 µm and the assigned pairs' 8.5 µm, and on synthetic data only 25–33% of assigned pairs are correct — most leftovers are nuclei with no Xenium cell (over-segmentation, or outside the Xenium plane). Large cells can hold a nucleus far off-centre, so some assigned pairs will be right; centroids alone can't say which. Filter on registration_status / neighbour_deviation, or pass --no-assign-remaining.

The output CSV holds the snapped positions in x_transformed / y_transformed, the smooth-transform positions in *_smooth, a registration_status (snapped / assigned / filled / unmoved), the partner's row in target_index and neighbour_deviation. Use --no-refine (or refine=False) for the smooth transform alone.

A snapped nucleus has zero residual by construction

So its TRE says nothing about whether it is on the right cell. The check is refinement["validation"]: a tenth of the accepted pairs is left out, their positions are predicted from their neighbours alone, and the error is reported. On z5 that is a median 4.0 µm — the nucleus-in-cell scatter that only individual snapping removes.

docs.title: Measuring quality honestly
docs.text:
Target Registration Error is easy to compute in a way that is circular. Correspondences here are established by nearest neighbour, so a sufficiently flexible transform can drive TRE to ~0 on the pairs it was fitted to, regardless of whether those correspondences are correct. An unregularised TPS with as many control points as pairs will always report TRE ≈ 0 on those pairs — that is interpolation, not accuracy.

register_centroids therefore always holds data out of fitting and reports TRE on it. The single-round methods hold out matched pairs; multiround re-estimates correspondences each round, so it holds out a quarter of the nuclei before anything is matched:

tre_initial      before any transform
tre_fit          on the data used for fitting      <- not evidence
tre_validation   on held-out data                  <- the real number

For multiround, TRE is the distance from each held-out nucleus to its mutual nearest cell. result["validation"] adds a correspondence-free summary of the held-out nuclei before and after: median distance to the nearest cell, and the fractions matched within 5 and 10 µm.

A large gap between fit and validation means the transform is memorising correspondences; a validation TRE no better than the initial one means it did not help. The function warns in both cases.

Matching is mutual by default

mutual=True keeps only pairs that are each other's nearest neighbour. One-directional matching lets many source points collapse onto a single popular target, inflating the pair count. On a real Venture 5 section this was the difference between 75,146 apparent pairs and 40,135 real ones.

docs.title: Interpreting the result
docs.text:
• A single-round method doesn't beat the initial TRE. Usually the starting offset is close to the cell spacing and nearest-neighbour matching is pairing nuclei with neighbouring cells. Use multiround.
  • Compare with the target's cell spacing. A residual that is a large fraction of it means many "matches" are neighbouring cells, not the same cell.
  • Expect a floor of a few microns. Xenium reports cell centroids; a stained nucleus's centroid is legitimately a few microns away from its cell's.
  • Sweep max_distance. If TRE shrinks in proportion rather than reaching a plateau, the threshold is setting the residual, not alignment error.

docs.title: Running on HPC
docs.text:
Registration can be submitted to SLURM or run locally through a job spec; see HPC Deployment and the napari plugin.

from smint.alignment.jobs import JobSpec, SlurmResources, submit, poll

spec = JobSpec(
    round="st_sm",
    inputs={"st_file": ..., "sm_file": ..., "st_points": ..., "sm_points": ...},
    params={"niter": 1000},
    output_dir="/vast/scratch/you/run1",
    backend="sbatch",
    resources=SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type="A30", memory="64G"),
)
info = submit(spec)
print(poll(spec.output_dir)["state"])

Batch jobs need shared storage

An sbatch job runs on a different machine, so node-local paths (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm) are invisible to it — the job dies with no logs at all, because the log directory does not exist there. JobSpec.validate() rejects these up front. Use /vast/scratch or /vast/projects.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
LDDMM runs on GPU automatically when one is available. Request it with SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1). GPU and CPU results are bit-identical; on a Venture 5 Z2 section the GPU run took 82 s against 112 s on 8 CPU cores, so the benefit is modest at typical raster sizes.

gpuq mixes A30, A100 and P100 cards, and a bare --gres=gpu:1 takes whatever is free — so an untyped request can land on hardware generations apart from the one a run was timed on. gpu_type defaults to "A30", the card registration is validated against, and renders as --gres=gpu:A30:1. Pass another name to pick a different card, or gpu_type=None to accept any:

SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type="A100")  # --gres=gpu:A100:1
SlurmResources(partition="gpuq", gpus=1, gpu_type=None)    # --gres=gpu:1

Types are checked against the partition before submission, so a card that partition does not have is reported by name rather than as SLURM's "Invalid generic resource". An unknown partition likewise raises with the list of valid ones. To see what the cluster offers:

from smint.alignment.jobs import available_partitions, available_gpu_types
available_partitions()          # via sinfo; [] off-cluster
available_gpu_types("gpuq")     # e.g. ['A100', 'A30', 'P100']

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
STalign requires numpy < 2 — the nptyping dependency it pulls in via nrrd uses np.object0, which numpy 2 removed. The centroid and pre-registration paths have no STalign dependency and run anywhere.

If stalign_available() returns False, check numpy first:

from smint.alignment import stalign_available
print(stalign_available())

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: SMINT uses YAML configuration files to control various aspects of the processing pipeline. This page explains how to configure SMINT for your specific needs.

docs.title: Configuration File Structure
docs.text:
SMINT configuration files are written in YAML format and have the following structure:

```yaml

docs.title: Base configuration
docs.text: output_dir: "results/segmentation" tile_info_path: "results/segmentation/current_tile_info.txt" live_update_image_path: "results/segmentation/live_view.png"

docs.title: Distributed processing
docs.text: use_gpu: true n_workers: null # null = use all available workers chunk_size: [2048, 2048] memory_limit: "16GB"

docs.title: Model paths
docs.text: model_paths: - "cyto" # Built-in Cellpose model for cytoplasm - "nuclei" # Built-in Cellpose model for nuclei # - "/path/to/custom/model" # Path to a custom model

docs.title: Cell segmentation parameters
docs.text: cell_model_params: diameter: 120.0 flow_threshold: 0.4 cellprob_threshold: -1.5 channels: [1, 2] # [cytoplasm, nucleus]

docs.title: Nuclear segmentation parameters
docs.text: nuclei_model_params: diameter: 40.0 flow_threshold: 0.4 cellprob_threshold: -1.2 channels: [2, 0] # [nucleus, no second channel]

docs.title: Adaptive nuclear segmentation
docs.text: adaptive_nuclei: enable: false cellprob_lower_limit: -6.0 step_decrement: 0.2 max_attempts: 3 trigger_ratio: 0.05

docs.title: Preprocessing options
docs.text: preprocessing: sigma: 1.0 # Gaussian blur sigma normalize: true channel_names: - "DAPI" - "AF568" - "AF647"

docs.title: Visualization options
docs.text: visualization: enable: true output_dir: "results/segmentation/visualizations" num_chunks_to_visualize: 5 roi_size: [2024, 2024] background_channel_indices: [0, 1] # Channels to use for visualization background

docs.title: Dependency Handling
docs.text: SMINT is designed with graceful dependency handling to ensure robust operation across different environments, even when some optional dependencies are missing.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
The core design principles for dependency handling in SMINT are:

  1. Graceful Degradation: The package should continue to function with reduced capabilities when optional dependencies are missing.
  2. Clear Feedback: Users should receive informative messages about missing dependencies and their impact.
  3. Minimal Core Requirements: The essential functionality should work with a minimal set of dependencies.
  4. Easy Extension: Adding optional dependencies should enable additional features without code changes.

docs.title: Detection Mechanism
docs.text:
SMINT uses a consistent pattern across all modules to detect and handle optional dependencies:

# Check for optional dependency
try:
    import some_package
    SOME_PACKAGE_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
    SOME_PACKAGE_AVAILABLE = False
    logging.warning("some_package not available. Some functionality will be limited.")

docs.title: Implementation Pattern
docs.text:
Functions that require optional dependencies check their availability before execution:

def function_requiring_dependency():
    if not SOME_PACKAGE_AVAILABLE:
        logging.error("This function requires some_package to be installed.")
        return {"error": "Missing required dependency: some_package"}

    # Normal function implementation
    ...

docs.title: Segmentation Module
docs.text: Dependency Required For Fallback Behavior cellpose Cell segmentation models Error message with installation instructions opencv-python Image I/O and contour extraction Limited visualization, no mask saving/loading dask[distributed] Distributed processing Single-process implementation only dask-cuda GPU acceleration CPU-only implementation

docs.title: Visualization Module
docs.text: Dependency Required For Fallback Behavior matplotlib All plotting functionality Error message with installation instructions opencv-python Image I/O and processing Limited visualization capabilities tkinter Live Scan Viewer GUI Command-line only interface

docs.title: R Integration Module
docs.text: Dependency Required For Fallback Behavior rpy2 Direct R integration Fallback to subprocess R script execution pandas Data transfer between Python and R Required dependency R (system) All R functionality Error message with installation instructions

docs.title: Checking Dependency Status
docs.text:
You can check the status of optional dependencies programmatically:

import importlib

def check_dependency(package_name):
    try:
        importlib.import_module(package_name)
        return True
    except ImportError:
        return False

# Check for cellpose
cellpose_available = check_dependency("cellpose")
print(f"Cellpose available: {cellpose_available}")

# Check for opencv
opencv_available = check_dependency("cv2")
print(f"OpenCV available: {opencv_available}")

# Check for rpy2
rpy2_available = check_dependency("rpy2")
print(f"rpy2 available: {rpy2_available}")

docs.title: Warnings and Error Messages
docs.text:
SMINT provides detailed warnings and error messages when dependencies are missing:

  1. Import-time warnings: When SMINT is imported, it will log warnings about missing optional dependencies.
  2. Function-specific errors: Functions that require missing dependencies will provide clear error messages.
  3. Installation instructions: Error messages include instructions for installing missing dependencies.

docs.title: Customizing Error Handling
docs.text:
You can customize the behavior when dependencies are missing by modifying the logging configuration:

import logging

# Set logging level to ERROR to suppress warnings about missing dependencies
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.ERROR)

# Or capture logs to a file
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s',
    filename='smint.log'
)

docs.title: Best Practices for Dependency Management
docs.text:
1. Install only what you need: Use selective installation to minimize dependencies: 

    pip install "smint[segmentation]"  # Only install segmentation dependencies

  2. Check availability before calling functions: 

    import smint
from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

# Check if distributed processing is available
try:
   import distributed
   distributed_available = True
except ImportError:
   distributed_available = False

# Use appropriate function based on availability
if distributed_available:
   result = run_distributed_segmentation(...)
else:
   result = smint.segmentation.process_large_image(...)

  3. Provide feedback to users: When building applications on top of SMINT, forward dependency warnings to users.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Worked examples on real data from the BCRL Venture cohort, run on the WEHI Milton cluster. Timings and results are from those runs; your numbers will depend on the data and hardware.

To try the API without any of these datasets, run the synthetic examples shipped with the repository:

python examples/alignment_example.py    # pre-registration, centroid fitting, job specs

docs.title: 1. Spatial metabolomics → spatial transcriptomics
docs.text:
MALDI spatial metabolomics (SM) acquired on a section neighbouring a Xenium spatial transcriptomics (ST) section. The tissue differs between sections, so this uses STalign LDDMM guided by manual landmarks.

Venture 5, Xenium section Z2 and MALDI section Ven5B. 459,969 SM pixels, 53,622 ST cells, 11 landmark pairs.

Inputs

File Contents Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv Xenium cells; registration uses x_final / y_final (auto-detected) Ven5B_information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv MALDI pixels: x, y and one column per m/z (442 MB) ven5_z2_st_points_B_points.npy, ven5_z2_sm_points_B_points.npy 11 paired landmarks

docs.title: Step 1 — rasterise both modalities for landmarking
docs.text:
from smint.alignment import prepare_landmark_inputs

out = prepare_landmark_inputs(
    st_file="Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv",
    sm_file="Ven5B_information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv",
    output_prefix="ven5_z2",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=10.0, rotate_left_90=True),   # MALDI pixels -> microns
)

docs.title: Step 2 — place landmarks
docs.text: Open the two datasets in the napari plugin (Plugins → SMINT Registration → 3. Landmarks), or run STalign's point_annotator.py on the two .npz files. Pick the same features in the same order in both; correspondence is positional.

docs.title: Step 3 — register on a GPU node
docs.text:
smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv \
    --sm Ven5B_information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv \
    --st-points ven5_z2_st_points_B_points.npy \
    --sm-points ven5_z2_sm_points_B_points.npy \
    --rotate-left-90 --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir /vast/scratch/$USER/ven5_z2 \
    --submit --watch --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --memory 64G \
    --worker-python /path/to/STalign_env/bin/python

submitted st_sm via sbatch (30527655)
state: completed -- st_sm round finished
{"transformed_csv": "/vast/scratch/.../ven5_z2/sm_transformed.csv"}

The worker ran LDDMM (1,000 iterations) on one A30; from submission to finished output, including queueing, took 72 s. The output keeps every m/z column and adds x_transformed / y_transformed.

The same run from Python:

from smint.alignment import register_sm_to_st

sm = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file="Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv",
    sm_file="Ven5B_information_matrix_tissue_only_full_with_xy.csv",
    st_points_file="ven5_z2_st_points_B_points.npy",
    sm_points_file="ven5_z2_sm_points_B_points.npy",
    sm_kwargs=dict(scale_xy=10.0, rotate_left_90=True),
    orientation="stalign",
    output_path="sm_transformed.csv",
)

Pass orientation=\"stalign\" to overlay on ST

The default, "dataset", reproduces historical outputs but is transposed relative to the ST cells. Plotted over ST it looks like a failed registration. See Coordinate orientation.

docs.title: Step 4 — check the result
docs.text:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

st = pd.read_csv("Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv", usecols=["x_final", "y_final"]).to_numpy()
sm = pd.read_csv("sm_transformed.csv", usecols=["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]).to_numpy()
d, _ = cKDTree(st).query(sm)
print(f"median distance to nearest ST cell: {np.median(d):.1f} um")

median distance to nearest ST cell: 16.4 um

That is about half a 30 µm MALDI pixel. Because the sections differ, there is no ground truth to score against; this distance and the overlay are the practical checks.

docs.title: 2. Coarse pre-registration with an orientation search
docs.text:
Before landmarking, bring a dataset roughly into the target frame. MALDI pixels from Ven5B (converted to microns) arrive rotated relative to the Z2 Xenium cells:

smint-alignment pretransform \
    --source ven5b_sm_xy.csv --target Z2_final_aligned_annos.csv \
    --search --output ven5b_pre.csv

INFO smint.cli.align: Best: rotation=90 flip_x=False flip_y=False
scale        : 1.2161, 1.2161
rotation     : 90.00 deg
reflects     : False
overlap      : 0.954
wrote        : ven5b_pre.csv
transform    : ven5b_pre.csv.transform.json

--search tries every 15° rotation with and without each flip and keeps the best overlap score. Here it recovered the 90° rotation that the Ven5B pipeline otherwise applies by hand (rotate_left_90=True), in 52 s for 459,969 pixels. The matrix and its decomposition are saved next to the output, so the step can be reproduced exactly. The napari plugin's 2. Pre-register widget does the same interactively.

docs.title: 3. Same-section registration: nuclei onto Xenium cells
docs.text:
When a second modality is acquired on the same section — here, nuclei segmented from a post-Xenium stain of Venture 5 section z5 — centroids correspond one-to-one:

smint-alignment centroid \
    --source transformed_nuc_points_in_global.csv --source-cols x_centroid y_centroid \
    --target z5_pre_aligned_coordinates.csv \
    --output-dir /vast/scratch/$USER/z5_nuc_to_xenium

{
  "method": "multiround",
  "n_matched": 49206,
  "tre_initial": 10.96,
  "tre_fit": 4.45,
  "tre_validation": 4.93,
  "refinement": {"n_snapped": 57083, "n_assigned": 8266, "n_filled": 9147,
                 "fraction_targets_matched": 0.88,
                 "median_deviation": {"snapped": 4.14, "assigned": 8.54},
                 "snapped_per_pass": [55208, 56923, 57069, 57083]},
  "rounds": [
    {"stage": "initial", "median_nn": 12.40},
    {"stage": "affine", "block_size": 500.0, "blocks": 300, "consistent_blocks": 0.91,
     "median_nn": 5.38, "accepted": true},
    {"stage": "tps", "block_size": 250.0, "blocks": 1013, "consistent_blocks": 0.77,
     "median_nn": 5.43, "accepted": false}
  ]
}

88,906 nuclei and 74,247 Xenium cells, about 17 µm apart; 3 s.

How to read this. tre_validation is measured on a quarter of the nuclei held out before any matching, and is the number to trust for the transform: 11.0 µm → 4.9 µm. The rounds show the affine voting round did the work; the finer TPS round didn't improve the fitting nuclei, so it was rejected.

Registration is then refined: 57,083 nuclei snap exactly onto distinct Xenium cells over four pairing passes, each checked against its neighbourhood, and 8,266 more are assigned to the free cells around them — 88% of Xenium cells now carry a nucleus. The assigned pairs deviate twice as much from their neighbourhood (8.5 µm against 4.1 µm), so treat them as unverified; the output CSV's registration_status and neighbour_deviation say which is which. See Snapping matched nuclei.

The single-round methods can't do this: they match each nucleus to its nearest cell before fitting, and with a starting offset close to the cell spacing most of those matches are wrong. --method ransac+tps only reaches 11.5 µm here. See Why multiple rounds.

docs.title: 4. Segmenting a whole-slide image on one GPU
docs.text:
A fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model segments cells, and Cellpose's base model segments nuclei, chunk by chunk:

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image

results = process_large_image(
    image_path="r6_crop.ome.tif",            # (C, Y, X): ch0 nuclei, ch1 GFAP
    csv_base_path="seg/r6",
    chunk_size=(1024, 1024),
    cell_model_path="/path/to/models/cpsam_20260225_153049",
    cells_diameter=120, cells_flow_threshold=0.6, cells_cellprob_threshold=-2.5,
    cells_channels=[2, 1],                  # main = channel 2 (GFAP), nuclear = channel 1
    nuclei_model_path="nuclei",             # Cellpose 4: falls back to cpsam, with a warning
    nuclei_diameter=25, nuclei_flow_threshold=0.3, nuclei_cellprob_threshold=0.2,
    nuclei_channels=[1, 0],
    visualize=True, visualize_output_dir="seg/vis",
)
print(results["total_cells"], results["total_nuclei"])

33 29

Venture 6, one 1024 px chunk of a 2048 × 2048 px crop; Cellpose 4 on one A30 took 23 s for the crop. Cyan: nuclei; green: GFAP; magenta: phalloidin. Right: cell outlines (white) and nucleus outlines (yellow).

channels follows Cellpose 3's convention ([main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none) and selects the same input on Cellpose 3 and 4.

docs.title: 5. Distributed segmentation on SLURM GPUs
docs.text:
For a whole slide, tiles are spread across GPU workers that SMINT launches through SLURM, then stitched and reconciled:

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="Venture6_tile_scan_R6.ome.tif",       # OME-TIFF or OME-Zarr, on shared storage
    output_dir="/vast/scratch/me/r6_seg",
    cell_model="/path/to/models/cpsam_20260225_153049",
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    cell_params={"diameter": 120, "flow_threshold": 0.6,
                 "cellprob_threshold": -2.5, "channels": [2, 1]},
    nuclei_params={"diameter": 25, "flow_threshold": 0.3,
                   "cellprob_threshold": 0.2, "channels": [1, 0]},
    chunk_size=1048, tile_overlap=256,
    backend="slurm", n_workers=4,
    slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30", "memory": "64GB"},
)

Tiles: 16 of 1048 px, 256 px overlap
4 worker(s) ready
Stitched 66 polygons: 44 after merging, 44 after trim/remove
30 of 103 cell outlines touch no nucleus and were dropped
Stitched 73 polygons: 43 after merging, 43 after trim/remove
Reconciled 43 cells / 44 nuclei -> 44 cells / 44 nuclei
Done in 0.6 min

Run the coordinator itself as a small CPU job (sbatch on regular); it submits the GPU workers and only stitches. The output directory then holds cells_outlines.csv / nuclei_outlines.csv (outline vertices), cells_summary.csv / nuclei_summary.csv (centroids, areas, and which cell each nucleus belongs to) and full-resolution label masks. See Segmentation for how tiles are stitched.

docs.title: HPC Deployment
docs.text: SMINT is designed to run efficiently on High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters, taking advantage of multiple CPUs and GPUs for processing large spatial omics datasets. This page explains how to deploy SMINT on SLURM-based HPC systems.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Running SMINT on an HPC cluster involves the following steps:

  1. Install SMINT on the HPC system
  2. Prepare your configuration file
  3. Submit jobs using SLURM submission scripts
  4. Monitor job progress
  5. Collect and analyze results

docs.title: Using Environment Modules
docs.text:
Most HPC systems use environment modules. Load the required modules and install SMINT:

```bash

docs.title: Load required modules
docs.text: module load python/3.11 module load cuda/11.3 module load miniconda3

docs.title: Create a conda environment
docs.text: conda create -n smint python=3.11 conda activate smint

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This guide covers the installation of SMINT and its dependencies.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
SMINT requires the following:

  • Python 3.8 or higher
  • CUDA toolkit (for GPU support, optional)
  • R 4.0 or higher (for R integration, optional)

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
• Memory: At least 16GB RAM, 32GB+ recommended for large images
  • CPU: Multi-core processor (8+ cores recommended)
  • GPU: NVIDIA GPU with at least 8GB VRAM (for GPU-accelerated segmentation, optional)
  • Storage: Depends on your image sizes, but typically 100GB+ free space

docs.title: Installation Methods
docs.text: SMINT is not published on PyPI — the smint name there is an unrelated placeholder, so pip install smint will not install this package. Install from GitHub instead.

docs.title: Option 1: Install from GitHub
docs.text: pip install "git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

docs.title: Option 2: Install from Source
docs.text:
For development or to contribute to the project:

git clone https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git
cd SMINT
pip install -e .

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: SMINT is designed with a modular approach to dependencies. Core functionality will work with minimal dependencies, while optional features require additional packages.

docs.title: Core Dependencies (Automatically Installed)
docs.text:
These dependencies are automatically installed when you install SMINT:

  • numpy: For numerical operations
  • pandas: For data manipulation
  • matplotlib: For visualization
  • dask: For parallel computing (base package)
  • scikit-image: For image processing
  • tifffile: For reading/writing OME-TIFF files
  • cellpose (3 or 4): For cell segmentation models
  • opencv-python: For image processing and contour extraction

Cellpose 3 and 4

SMINT works with Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4. Models are given as a built-in name or a path to a trained model. Cellpose 3 has the cyto, cyto2, cyto3 and nuclei models; Cellpose 4 has only Cellpose-SAM (cpsam), so on Cellpose 4 those names fall back to cpsam with a warning — pass a fine-tuned model path instead. channels ([main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none) selects the input channels identically on both versions.

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text: These dependencies enable additional features but are not required for core functionality:

docs.title: Distributed Processing
docs.text:
• smint[distributed]: Dask distributed, dask-jobqueue (SLURM workers), zarr and shapely, for run_distributed_segmentation 

    pip install "smint[distributed] @ git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

  • dask-cuda: One local worker per GPU (requires CUDA) 

    pip install dask-cuda

docs.title: R Integration
docs.text:
• rpy2: For direct R integration 
    pip install rpy2

docs.title: Installation with All Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
To install SMINT with all optional dependencies:

pip install "smint[all] @ git+https://github.com/JurgenKriel/SMINT.git"

Or selectively, from a source checkout:

pip install -e ".[r_integration]"  # For R integration features
pip install -e ".[docs]"           # To build this documentation
pip install -e ".[dev]"            # pytest, flake8, black

Registration with STalign also needs STalign itself, which is installed separately and requires numpy < 2 (see Alignment):

pip install --upgrade "git+https://github.com/JEFworks-Lab/STalign.git"

docs.title: napari Plugin
docs.text:
SMINT ships a napari plugin for the interactive parts of registration: loading datasets, pre-registering them by eye, placing landmarks, and launching the registration itself as a batch or local job.

Launch napari from an environment that has both napari and SMINT, then open Plugins → SMINT Registration.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The plugin never imports STalign. Registration is handed to a separate worker interpreter through a job spec on disk:

┌─ napari process ─────────────────────────────┐
│  load → pre-register → landmarks → submit     │
│  writes *_points.npy + job_spec.json          │
└───────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                │  sbatch  │  or  local subprocess
┌───────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐
│  worker (STalign_env)                         │
│  smint-register → registration → status.json  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is not incidental. napari and napari_spatialdata need numpy ≥ 2, while STalign requires numpy < 2 — they cannot share a process. Passing a job spec between them sidesteps that entirely, keeps the viewer responsive during a multi-minute LDDMM, and means a failed registration cannot take napari down.

Point the worker at a suitable interpreter with:

export SMINT_WORKER_PYTHON=/path/to/STalign_env/bin/python

Otherwise SMINT looks for an STalign_env beside the installed package, then falls back to the current interpreter.

docs.title: 1. Load datasets
docs.text:
Reads a source/target pair into Points layers, optionally with a smoothed density Image for anatomical context.

Coordinate columns are auto-detected across the conventions in use — x_final/y_final (ST annotations), x_centroid/y_centroid (Xenium), centroid_x/centroid_y (segmented nuclei), or plain x/y.

Only coordinate columns are read, and display is capped at 200,000 points. Neither affects registration, which always reads the full file in the worker.

docs.title: 2. Pre-register
docs.text:
Scale, rotate and flip the source onto the target's coordinate system before landmarking. Adjustments update a preview layer live.

  • Rotation — slider, degrees counter-clockwise
  • Flip horizontally / vertically
  • Scale — extent (match bounding-box spans), max (match maxima), none, or manual
  • Search rotation/flip — grid search over orientations, scored by overlap

The status line reports an overlap score (0–1, fraction of occupied target bins the source also occupies). It needs no correspondences, so it is fast enough to update as you drag a slider — a full registration per adjustment would not be.

Apply and save writes the transformed CSV plus a .pretransform.json recording the matrix and its decomposition, so a coarse transform can be reproduced later instead of being an unrecorded manual step.

docs.title: 3. Landmarks
docs.text:
Creates paired SM landmarks / ST landmarks Points layers. Place landmarks with napari's native Points tool directly on the data, in real-world units — there is no raster grid and so no pixel-to-micron conversion in the registration path.

Order is the correspondence

Pick the same anatomical features in the same order in both layers. Correspondence is positional; an ordering mismatch silently produces a wrong registration rather than an error.

Check pairing validates counts and the three-pair minimum an affine needs. Save landmark pair writes <prefix>_sm_points.npy and <prefix>_st_points.npy in exactly the format STalign's point_annotator.py uses, so plugin output and existing landmark files are interchangeable.

docs.title: 4. Register
docs.text:
Builds a job spec and submits it.

Field Applies to Round st_sm (needs landmarks) or centroid Run via sbatch or local Method, Max match distance centroid round LDDMM iterations st_sm round Partition / CPUs / Memory / Time limit sbatch only

Progress is polled in a background thread, so the viewer stays usable. On completion the transformed points are added as a new layer and the held-out TRE is reported; on failure the error is surfaced as a notification.

Batch jobs need shared storage

An sbatch job runs on a different machine, so node-local paths (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm) are unreachable — the job dies with no logs at all, because the log directory does not exist there. SMINT rejects these before submitting. Use /vast/scratch or /vast/projects.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
Request a GPU with a GPU partition and gpus=1. LDDMM uses CUDA automatically when available, and GPU results are bit-identical to CPU. The speedup is modest at typical raster sizes — 82 s versus 112 s on 8 CPU cores for a Venture 5 section — so CPU is a perfectly reasonable default.

GPU type picks the card. gpuq holds a mix of A30, A100 and P100, and "any" takes whichever is free, so a run can land on a much older card than the one it was timed on. It defaults to the A30, which registration is validated against. The dropdown lists what the cluster actually advertises.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Widget fails with missing 1 required positional argument: 'viewer' napari only injects the viewer into QWidget/magicgui Widget subclasses and MagicFactory instances. A plain function contribution is called with no arguments. Widgets needing the viewer must be classes.

Plugin does not appear in the Plugins menu Reinstall so the napari.manifest entry point is registered:

pip install -e . --no-deps --no-build-isolation

stalign_available() is False in the napari environment Expected — napari environments run numpy ≥ 2. The worker interpreter is what needs STalign, not napari. The centroid and pre-registration paths work in either.

docs.title: R Integration
docs.text: SMINT provides seamless integration with R for spatial omics data analysis, allowing you to leverage existing R packages within your Python workflow.

docs.text: ```python from smint.r_integration import run_r_script

docs.text:

print(f"Script completed with return code: {return_code}")

docs.title: Cell Segmentation
docs.text: SMINT provides powerful tools for segmenting cells and nuclei in whole-slide images, with support for distributed processing and multiple GPUs. This comprehensive guide covers all aspects of the segmentation pipeline, from data preparation to post-processing.

docs.title: Overview of Segmentation Pipeline
docs.text:
The SMINT segmentation pipeline consists of several key stages:

  1. Image Preprocessing - Preparing and normalizing input images
  2. Cell Segmentation - Identifying whole cells using Cellpose
  3. Nuclei Segmentation - Identifying cell nuclei (optional)
  4. Post-processing - Refining segmentation results and extracting features
  5. Visualization - Generating visual outputs for quality control

Venture 6 brain tissue: nuclei (cyan), GFAP (green) and phalloidin (magenta), with cell outlines (white) and nucleus outlines (yellow) from a fine-tuned Cellpose-SAM model on one GPU. See Examples for the code.

docs.title: Supported Image Formats
docs.text: SMINT supports the following image formats: - OME-TIFF (preferred) - Multi-channel, multi-resolution format with metadata - TIFF - Standard format, single or multi-channel - CZI - Carl Zeiss format; export tiles first (see segmentation/export_czi_tile_coordinates.ipynb)

docs.title: Required Image Properties
docs.text:
For optimal segmentation results, input images should have: - Resolution: Ideally 0.5-1 μm/pixel for cell segmentation, 0.25-0.5 μm/pixel for nuclei - Channels: - At least one membrane/cytoplasm channel (e.g., WGA, phalloidin) - At least one nuclear channel (e.g., DAPI, Hoechst) for nuclei segmentation - Bit depth: 8-bit or 16-bit grayscale per channel - Quality: Minimal noise, good contrast between cells and background

Cellpose 3 and 4

SMINT works with Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4. Models are given as a built-in name or a path to a trained model. Cellpose 3 has the cyto, cyto2, cyto3 and nuclei models; Cellpose 4 has only Cellpose-SAM (cpsam), so on Cellpose 4 those names fall back to cpsam with a warning — pass a fine-tuned model path instead. channels ([main, nuclear], 1-based, 0 = none) selects the input channels identically on both versions.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Segmentation is run with scripts/run_segmentation.py from a source checkout. Model parameters (thresholds, channels, adaptive nuclei settings) come from a YAML config — see Configuration and configs/segmentation_config.yaml.

docs.title: Single-Process Segmentation
docs.text:
python scripts/run_segmentation.py \
    --image path/to/image.ome.tiff \
    --output-dir results/segmentation \
    --config configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --cell-diameter 60 \
    --nuclei-diameter 30 \
    --visualize

docs.title: Distributed Segmentation
docs.text:
Add --distributed to split the image into overlapping tiles segmented in parallel by Dask workers, and --use-gpu to use GPU workers (needs pip install "smint[distributed]"):

python scripts/run_segmentation.py \
    --image path/to/large_image.ome.tiff \
    --output-dir results/segmentation \
    --config configs/segmentation_config.yaml \
    --distributed \
    --use-gpu \
    --chunk-size 2048 2048

docs.title: Command-Line Options
docs.text: Option Description Default --image Path to input image Required --output-dir Directory to save results Required --config YAML configuration file Built-in defaults --distributed Run in distributed mode using Dask Off --use-gpu Use GPU for computation (distributed mode; single-process uses the GPU when Cellpose finds one) Off --cell-model Cell model: built-in name (e.g. cyto) or path to a custom model From config --nuclei-model Nuclei model: built-in name (e.g. nuclei) or path to a custom model From config --cell-diameter Expected cell diameter in pixels From config --nuclei-diameter Expected nuclei diameter in pixels From config --chunk-size Chunk height and width 2048 2048 --visualize Generate visualizations Off --live-viewer Write live-view images for the live viewer Off --save-config Save the effective configuration to the output directory Off --debug Enable debug logging Off

docs.title: Segmentation API
docs.text:
For programmatic usage within Python scripts:

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image

# Basic usage
results = process_large_image(
    image_path="path/to/image.ome.tiff",
    csv_base_path="results/segmentation",
    chunk_size=(2048, 2048),
    # Cell parameters
    cell_model_path="cyto",
    cells_diameter=80.0,
    cells_flow_threshold=0.4,
    cells_cellprob_threshold=-1.5,
    cells_channels=[0, 0],  # [channel, 0] for grayscale, [channel1, channel2] for RGB
    # Nuclei parameters
    nuclei_model_path="nuclei",
    nuclei_diameter=40.0,
    nuclei_flow_threshold=0.4,
    nuclei_cellprob_threshold=-1.5,
    nuclei_channels=[1, 0],  # [channel, 0] for grayscale
    # Visualization
    visualize=True,
    visualize_output_dir="results/visualization",
    num_visualize_chunks=5,
    visualize_roi_size=(512, 512)
)

# Access the results
print(results["total_cells"], results["total_nuclei"])
cells_csv = results["cells_csv_path"]     # <csv_base_path>_cells.csv
nuclei_csv = results["nuclei_csv_path"]   # <csv_base_path>_nuclei.csv

For distributed processing:

from smint.segmentation import run_distributed_segmentation

results = run_distributed_segmentation(
    image_path="path/to/large_image.ome.zarr",   # OME-Zarr, Zarr, TIFF or OME-TIFF
    output_dir="/vast/scratch/you/seg_run",      # shared storage for SLURM workers
    config_path="configs/segmentation_config.yaml",
    cell_model="/path/to/cpsam_finetuned",        # model path or built-in name
    nuclei_model="nuclei",
    chunk_size=2048,                              # core tile size (px)
    tile_overlap=256,                             # > largest cell radius
    backend="slurm",                              # or "local"
    n_workers=8,
    slurm={"queue": "gpuq", "gpu_type": "A30", "memory": "64GB"},
)
print(results["total_cells"], results["cells_summary_path"])

backend="local" runs CPU workers, or one worker per GPU when dask-cuda is installed; scheduler_address= connects to an existing Dask cluster. The config file's optional distributed: section takes the same keys.

docs.title: Stitching tiles
docs.text:
Each tile is segmented with an overlap margin, so cells on a tile boundary are seen whole by both neighbours. The duplicates and collisions this creates are resolved with a port of the R workflow in stitching/stitching.Rmd (smint.segmentation.stitching). Overlap below is the intersection as a fraction of the smaller object.

  1. Stitch nuclei, then cells (cells must touch a stitched nucleus): merge pairs overlapping by more than 50% until nothing more merges, then trim overlaps under 25% from both objects, then drop the smaller object of any pair still overlapping by 25% or more.
  2. Reconcile cells with nuclei: drop cells without a credible nucleus, grow cells over nuclei they mostly contain, split nuclei straddling several cells, remove duplicate and contained objects, and assign every nucleus to exactly one cell. Nuclei with no cell become nucleus-only cells.

The thresholds are stitch_merge_thresh (0.5) and stitch_trim_thresh (0.25); reconcile_nuclei=False skips step 2.

docs.title: Advanced Adaptive Segmentation
docs.text:
SMINT supports adaptive segmentation that dynamically adjusts parameters based on local image characteristics:

from smint.segmentation import process_large_image

results = process_large_image(
    # Basic parameters as above, plus:
    enable_adaptive_nuclei=True,
    nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_lower_limit=-6.0,
    nuclei_adaptive_cellprob_step_decrement=0.2,
    nuclei_max_adaptive_attempts=3,
    adaptive_nuclei_trigger_ratio=0.05  # Retry if nuclei count < 5% of cells
)

docs.title: Output Files and Formats
docs.text:
process_large_image writes:

File Description Format <csv_base_path>_cells.csv Cell outline coordinates CSV with global_cell_id, x, y <csv_base_path>_nuclei.csv Nuclei outline coordinates CSV with global_cell_id, x, y chunk_<y>_<x>.png Per-chunk visualizations (with visualize=True) PNG live_update.png Latest chunk, for the live viewer PNG

run_distributed_segmentation writes, in output_dir:

File Description cells_outlines.csv, nuclei_outlines.csv Stitched outline vertices: global_cell_id, x, y cells_summary.csv Per cell: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, n_nuclei nuclei_summary.csv Per nucleus: global_cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, area, cell_id (containing cell) cells.zarr, nuclei.zarr Full-resolution label masks (per-tile IDs, not the stitched IDs)

docs.title: Live Segmentation Viewer
docs.text:
SMINT includes a Tkinter viewer for monitoring segmentation in real time. From the command line:

smint-viewer path/to/image.ome.tiff results/segmentation results/segmentation/current_tile_info.txt --interval 1000

Or from Python:

from smint.visualization import run_viewer

run_viewer(
    full_scan_path="path/to/image.ome.tiff",
    segmentation_history_dir="results/segmentation",
    tile_info_path="results/segmentation/current_tile_info.txt",
    update_interval_ms=1000,  # Update every 1 second
)

docs.title: Poor Segmentation Quality
docs.text:
• Problem: Cells or nuclei not properly detected
  • Solution: Adjust diameter, flow_threshold, and cellprob_threshold. Try using larger diameter for bigger cells, lower flow_threshold for weakly stained cells.

docs.title: Memory Errors
docs.text:
• Problem: "CUDA out of memory" or other memory-related errors
  • Solution: Reduce chunk_size, or use distributed processing with multiple GPUs.

docs.title: Processing Speed
docs.text:
• Problem: Segmentation taking too long
  • Solution: Use multi-GPU processing, reduce visualization, skip nuclei segmentation if not needed.

docs.title: Boundary Artifacts
docs.text:
• Problem: Cell masks cut off at chunk boundaries
  • Solution: Use larger chunks so fewer cells straddle a boundary.

docs.title: Performance Benchmarks

docs.title: Aligning Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics with Spatial Metabolomics
docs.text: This guide provides a detailed walkthrough for aligning 10X Xenium spatial transcriptomics data with spatial metabolomics data using STalign within the SMINT framework.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Integrating spatial transcriptomics data with spatial metabolomics presents unique challenges due to: - Different resolution and sampling density - Distinct coordinate systems - Potential tissue deformation between acquisitions - Different feature types (genes vs. metabolites)

The SMINT package leverages STalign (from the JEFworks Lab) to perform robust alignment using diffeomorphic transformations that can account for non-linear deformations between modalities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before beginning the alignment process, ensure you have:

  • 10X Xenium spatial transcriptomics data processed into a coordinate file
  • Spatial metabolomics data in matrix format with x,y coordinates
  • The STalign package installed (pip install STalign)
  • Sufficient computational resources (GPU recommended for large datasets)

docs.title: Spatial Metabolomics Data
docs.text:
The spatial metabolomics data should be in a CSV format with: - Row indices for unique spot/pixel identifiers - x and y columns for spatial coordinates - Additional columns for m/z values representing metabolite intensities

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def read_sm_matrix(mtx_file, verbose=True):
    """
    Read a Spatial Metabolomics matrix file and extract coordinates and data
    """
    if verbose:
        print("Reading matrix file...")

    try:
        data = pd.read_csv(mtx_file, index_col=0)
        numeric_cols = []
        for col in data.columns:
            try:
                numeric_cols.append(float(col))
            except ValueError:
                continue
    except Exception as e:
        raise Exception(f"Error reading matrix file: {e}")

    coordinates = data[['x', 'y']].values

    if verbose:
        print(f"Found {len(coordinates)} coordinate pairs")
        print(f"Found {len(numeric_cols)} m/z values")

    return coordinates, data, numeric_cols

docs.title: Xenium Data
docs.text:
Xenium data should be processed to extract cell centroids:

def read_xenium_data(xenium_file, verbose=True):
    """
    Read 10X Xenium data and extract cell coordinates
    """
    if verbose:
        print("Reading Xenium cell coordinates...")

    try:
        data = pd.read_csv(xenium_file)
        # Ensure the necessary columns exist
        required_cols = ['x_centroid', 'y_centroid']
        for col in required_cols:
            if col not in data.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"Required column '{col}' not found in Xenium data")
    except Exception as e:
        raise Exception(f"Error reading Xenium file: {e}")

    coordinates = data[['x_centroid', 'y_centroid']].values

    if verbose:
        print(f"Found {len(coordinates)} cell coordinates")

    return coordinates, data

docs.title: Step 2: Visualizing Data Before Alignment
docs.text:
Visualizing both datasets before alignment helps assess the initial misalignment and identify potential challenges:

def plot_non_zero_coordinates(coordinates, data, title="Coordinates Plot"):
    """
    Plot the coordinates of all non-zero m/z ratios for spatial metabolomics
    or all cell coordinates for Xenium data
    """
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))

    # For spatial metabolomics data
    if 'mz_values' in data.columns:
        mz_values = [float(col) for col in data.columns if col.replace('.', '').isdigit()]
        for mz in mz_values:
            column_name = str(mz)
            intensities = data[column_name].values

            # Filter coordinates where intensity is greater than zero
            non_zero_indices = np.where(intensities > 0)[0]
            filtered_coordinates = coordinates[non_zero_indices]

            # Plot non-zero coordinates
            plt.scatter(filtered_coordinates[:, 0], filtered_coordinates[:, 1], 
                        s=10, alpha=0.5, color='blue')
    else:
        # For Xenium data, plot all coordinates
        plt.scatter(coordinates[:, 0], coordinates[:, 1], 
                    s=10, alpha=0.5, color='red')

    plt.xlabel('X coordinate')
    plt.ylabel('Y coordinate')
    plt.title(title)
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.xlim(coordinates[:, 0].min() - 1, coordinates[:, 0].max() + 1)
    plt.ylim(coordinates[:, 1].min() - 1, coordinates[:, 1].max() + 1)
    plt.savefig(f"{title.replace(' ', '_')}.png", dpi=300)
    plt.show()

docs.title: Step 3: Rasterization
docs.text:
STalign works with rasterized (gridded) data. The rasterization step transforms point clouds into pixel-based representations:

import STalign

def rasterize_coordinates(x_coords, y_coords, pixel_size, verbose=True):
    """
    Convert point coordinates to a rasterized grid

    Parameters:
    -----------
    x_coords : numpy.ndarray
        X coordinates of the points
    y_coords : numpy.ndarray
        Y coordinates of the points
    pixel_size : float
        Size of the pixels in the rasterized grid
    verbose : bool
        Whether to display the rasterization result

    Returns:
    --------
    tuple
        (X grid, Y grid, intensity values, figure if verbose=True)
    """
    if verbose:
        print(f"Rasterizing {len(x_coords)} points with pixel size {pixel_size}")

    # Perform rasterization
    X_grid, Y_grid, intensity, fig = STalign.rasterize(x_coords, y_coords, dx=pixel_size)

    if verbose:
        print(f"Rasterized grid shape: {intensity.shape}")
        plt.savefig(f"rasterized_grid_size_{pixel_size}.png", dpi=300)
        plt.close(fig)

    return X_grid, Y_grid, intensity, fig if verbose else None

The pixel size parameter (dx) is critical: - Too small: Sparse representation with many empty pixels - Too large: Loss of spatial resolution and detail - Optimal: Usually determined empirically (start with 20-50µm for Xenium data)

docs.title: Step 4: Running LDDMM Alignment
docs.text:
The Large Deformation Diffeomorphic Metric Mapping (LDDMM) algorithm performs the alignment:

def run_lddmm_alignment(source_grid, target_grid, source_intensity, target_intensity, params=None):
    """
    Perform LDDMM alignment between source and target datasets

    Parameters:
    -----------
    source_grid : tuple
        (Y grid, X grid) for source data
    target_grid : tuple
        (Y grid, X grid) for target data
    source_intensity : numpy.ndarray
        Intensity values for source grid
    target_intensity : numpy.ndarray
        Intensity values for target grid
    params : dict, optional
        Parameters for LDDMM algorithm

    Returns:
    --------
    dict
        LDDMM output containing transformation parameters
    """
    # Default parameters if none provided
    if params is None:
        params = {
            'niter': 1000,  # Maximum iterations
            'diffeo_start': 50,  # Start diffeomorphic transformation earlier
            'sigmaM': 0.5,  # Kernel width for momentum field
            'sigmaB': 1.2,  # Kernel width for backward map
            'sigmaA': 1.2,  # Kernel width for forward map
            'epV': 500,     # Regularization parameter
        }

    # Check for GPU availability and set device
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        params['device'] = 'cuda:0'
        print("Using GPU for LDDMM calculation")
    else:
        params['device'] = 'cpu'
        print("Using CPU for LDDMM calculation (this may be slow)")

    # Run LDDMM
    print("Running LDDMM alignment...")
    output = STalign.LDDMM(
        source_grid,  # [Y_source, X_source]
        source_intensity,
        target_grid,  # [Y_target, X_target]
        target_intensity,
        **params
    )

    print("LDDMM alignment complete")
    return output

docs.title: Step 5: Transforming Point Coordinates
docs.text:
After obtaining the LDDMM transformation, apply it to transform the original spatial metabolomics coordinates:

def transform_points(lddmm_output, source_coordinates):
    """
    Transform source coordinates using LDDMM output

    Parameters:
    -----------
    lddmm_output : dict
        Output from the LDDMM alignment
    source_coordinates : numpy.ndarray
        Original source coordinates to transform (shape: n x 2)

    Returns:
    --------
    numpy.ndarray
        Transformed coordinates (shape: n x 2)
    """
    # Extract transformation parameters
    A = lddmm_output['A']
    v = lddmm_output['v']
    xv = lddmm_output['xv']

    # Ensure device is set correctly for tensor operations
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        torch.set_default_device('cuda:0')
    else:
        torch.set_default_device('cpu')

    # Stack y and x coordinates (note the order for STalign)
    stacked_coords = np.stack([source_coordinates[:, 1], source_coordinates[:, 0]], axis=1)

    # Apply transformation
    transformed_points = STalign.transform_points_source_to_target(xv, v, A, stacked_coords)
    transformed_points = transformed_points.cpu().numpy()

    # Return as [x, y] format
    return np.column_stack([transformed_points[:, 1], transformed_points[:, 0]])

docs.title: Step 6: Visualizing Alignment Results
docs.text:
Visualize the alignment to assess quality:

def visualize_alignment(xenium_coords, transformed_met_coords, output_path=None):
    """
    Visualize the alignment between Xenium and transformed metabolomics data

    Parameters:
    -----------
    xenium_coords : numpy.ndarray
        Xenium cell coordinates (shape: n x 2)
    transformed_met_coords : numpy.ndarray
        Transformed metabolomics coordinates (shape: m x 2)
    output_path : str, optional
        Path to save the visualization
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))

    # Plot Xenium coordinates
    ax.scatter(
        xenium_coords[:, 0], xenium_coords[:, 1],
        s=0.3, alpha=0.5, label='Xenium', color='blue'
    )

    # Plot transformed metabolomics coordinates
    ax.scatter(
        transformed_met_coords[:, 0], transformed_met_coords[:, 1],
        s=0.2, alpha=0.4, label='Transformed Metabolomics', color='orange'
    )

    ax.set_xlabel('X coordinate')
    ax.set_ylabel('Y coordinate')
    ax.set_title('Alignment of Xenium and Spatial Metabolomics Data')
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(True)

    if output_path:
        plt.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')

    plt.show()

docs.title: Step 7: Saving Transformed Coordinates
docs.text:
Save the transformed coordinates along with the original data:

def save_transformed_data(original_data, transformed_coords, output_path):
    """
    Save the original data with transformed coordinates

    Parameters:
    -----------
    original_data : pandas.DataFrame
        Original data with features
    transformed_coords : numpy.ndarray
        Transformed coordinates (shape: n x 2)
    output_path : str
        Path to save the combined data
    """
    # Ensure the number of rows match
    assert len(original_data) == len(transformed_coords), "Number of coordinates doesn't match data rows"

    # Create a copy of the original data
    result_df = original_data.copy()

    # Add transformed coordinates
    result_df['x_transformed'] = transformed_coords[:, 0]
    result_df['y_transformed'] = transformed_coords[:, 1]

    # Save to CSV
    result_df.to_csv(output_path, index=False)
    print(f"Saved transformed data to {output_path}")

docs.title: Complete Workflow Example
docs.text:
Here's a complete example that performs all the steps:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import STalign
import os

# Step 1: Read data
met_file = "path/to/metabolomics_data.csv"
xenium_file = "path/to/xenium_data.csv"

# Create output directory
output_dir = "alignment_results"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

# Read metabolomics data
met_coords, met_data, mz_values = read_sm_matrix(met_file)

# Read Xenium data
xenium_coords, xenium_data = read_xenium_data(xenium_file)

# Step 2: Visualize before alignment
plot_non_zero_coordinates(met_coords, met_data, "Spatial Metabolomics Coordinates")
plot_non_zero_coordinates(xenium_coords, xenium_data, "Xenium Cell Coordinates")

# Step 3: Rasterize both datasets
# Experiment with different pixel sizes
pixel_size = 30  # in the same units as your coordinates (usually µm)
X_met, Y_met, intensity_met, _ = rasterize_coordinates(
    met_coords[:, 0], met_coords[:, 1], pixel_size
)
X_xenium, Y_xenium, intensity_xenium, _ = rasterize_coordinates(
    xenium_coords[:, 0], xenium_coords[:, 1], pixel_size
)

# Step 4: Run LDDMM alignment
# Customize parameters based on your data
lddmm_params = {
    'niter': 1000,
    'diffeo_start': 50,
    'sigmaM': 0.5,
    'sigmaB': 1.2,
    'sigmaA': 1.2,
    'epV': 500,
}

lddmm_output = run_lddmm_alignment(
    [Y_met, X_met], [Y_xenium, X_xenium],
    intensity_met, intensity_xenium,
    params=lddmm_params
)

# Step 5: Transform metabolomics coordinates
transformed_met_coords = transform_points(lddmm_output, met_coords)

# Step 6: Visualize alignment results
output_plot_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "xenium_metabolomics_alignment.png")
visualize_alignment(xenium_coords, transformed_met_coords, output_plot_path)

# Step 7: Save transformed data
output_data_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "metabolomics_transformed.csv")
save_transformed_data(met_data, transformed_met_coords, output_data_path)

docs.title: Tuning the LDDMM Parameters
docs.text:
1. Pixel Size (dx):
  2. Start with a moderate value (20-50µm)
  3. Too small: Sparse representation
  4. Too large: Loss of detail

  5. Optimal: Balances detail and computational efficiency

  6. sigmaM, sigmaB, sigmaA (Kernel Width Parameters):

  7. Control the smoothness of the transformation
  8. Smaller values: Allow more local deformations
  9. Larger values: More global transformation, less flexibility

  10. Recommended approach: Start with defaults, then adjust if alignment quality is poor

  11. epV (Regularization Parameter):

  12. Controls the trade-off between data fitting and transformation smoothness
  13. Higher values: Smoother, more conservative transformations
  14. Lower values: More aggressive fitting, potentially more distortion
  15. Start with 500, increase if the transformation appears too distorted

docs.title: GPU vs. CPU Performance
docs.text:
• For large datasets (>10,000 points), GPU acceleration is strongly recommended
  • With GPU: Minutes to tens of minutes
  • Without GPU: Hours to days for large datasets

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. Poor Alignment Quality
  2. Check initial data quality and preprocessing
  3. Try different pixel sizes for rasterization
  4. Adjust LDDMM parameters, particularly sigmaM and epV

  5. Consider a rough manual pre-alignment if datasets are severely misaligned

  6. Memory Errors

  7. Reduce rasterization resolution (increase pixel size)
  8. Process subsets of the data

  9. Use a machine with more GPU memory

  10. Inverted or Flipped Alignment

  11. Pre-process your data to ensure consistent orientation

  12. Try flipping one dataset before alignment

  13. Alignment Fails to Converge

  14. Increase the number of iterations (niter)
  15. Try a simpler transformation first, then use that as initialization
  16. Check for outliers in your data
